subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Medieval Church & the Crusades
subtitle: The power of the Church in medieval life and the causes and consequences of the Crusades.

data.targetWord: a compulsory payment to the Church, usually understood as one tenth of a person's annual produce or income

examples.en-GB: Every parish family paid a tithe, which gave the Church a regular and substantial income.

data.targetWord: a holy ceremony in medieval Christianity believed to bring a person closer to God, such as baptism, confession, marriage or the Eucharist

examples.en-GB: People believed that receiving sacraments was essential for salvation and avoiding hell.

data.targetWord: a journey made to a holy place for religious reasons such as seeking forgiveness, healing or showing devotion to God or a saint

examples.en-GB: After Becket's murder, Canterbury became one of the most popular pilgrimage sites in England.

data.targetWord: the Church's most severe punishment, officially excluding a person from the Christian community and threatening their hope of salvation

examples.en-GB: Pope Innocent III excommunicated King John in 1209, damaging his authority as a Christian king.

data.targetWord: in medieval Catholic belief, a state after death where souls are cleansed of remaining sin before entering heaven

examples.en-GB: People donated money to the Church and paid for masses to reduce time their souls would spend in purgatory.

data.targetWord: an object believed to be physically connected to a saint or holy person, venerated by medieval Christians as a source of spiritual power

examples.en-GB: Pilgrims travelled to Canterbury to pray before the relics of Thomas Becket.

data.targetWord: a community where monks lived according to strict religious rules, combining daily prayer with work, scholarship and charitable duties

examples.en-GB: Medieval monasteries copied manuscripts, educated some children and cared for the sick and poor.

data.targetWord: the legal protection offered by a church building to any person who sought refuge there, preventing immediate arrest

examples.en-GB: A fugitive could claim sanctuary in a church and could not legally be removed by royal officers.

data.targetWord: the most senior bishop in a region, with authority over other bishops; in medieval England the Archbishop of Canterbury had great political and religious influence

examples.en-GB: Thomas Becket became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162 and soon clashed with Henry II.

data.targetWord: a person who is killed because of their religious beliefs or in defence of a cause, often venerated as a saint afterwards

examples.en-GB: Becket was declared a martyr and saint in 1173 after his murder in Canterbury Cathedral.

data.targetWord: a religious military expedition called by the Pope, sending western European Christians to fight for control of the Holy Land and other areas

examples.en-GB: Pope Urban II called the First Crusade in 1095, promising spiritual rewards to those who fought.

data.targetWord: the region around Jerusalem and other sites sacred to Christians, Muslims and Jews, which was the principal focus of the Crusades

examples.en-GB: The Crusaders captured Jerusalem, the holiest city in the Holy Land, in 1099.

data.targetWord: the head of the Roman Catholic Church in western Europe, whose spiritual authority allowed him to call Crusades, excommunicate rulers and influence Christian kingdoms

examples.en-GB: The Pope's ability to call the First Crusade demonstrated the enormous reach of his spiritual authority.

data.targetWord: the Muslim ruler who recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187 and became a renowned military leader in the Third Crusade

examples.en-GB: Saladin's recapture of Jerusalem in 1187 shocked Christian Europe and led to the Third Crusade.

data.targetWord: the Christian-controlled territories established in the eastern Mediterranean after the First Crusade, maintained by European nobles and castles

examples.en-GB: The Crusader States depended on trade, castles and ongoing support from western Europe to survive.

data.targetWord: men and women who had taken religious orders and served the Church, including priests, bishops, monks and nuns

examples.en-GB: The clergy had their own legal courts, which became a source of conflict between Henry II and Becket.

data.targetWord: a severe Church punishment that suspended most religious services in a kingdom, preventing people from receiving sacraments and putting pressure on the ruler

examples.en-GB: England was placed under interdict in 1208 during the dispute between John and the Pope.

data.targetWord: a reason or desire that drives a person to act; Crusaders had mixed motives including religious faith, desire for land and hopes of status

examples.en-GB: Historians agree that Crusaders had mixed motives: religion, land, honour and adventure all played a part.

data.targetWord: in Christian belief, being saved from sin and its consequences, allowing a person's soul to reach heaven rather than hell or purgatory

examples.en-GB: Fear of losing salvation made the Church's sacraments and rituals central to everyday medieval life.

data.targetWord: the local area served by one church and priest, forming the basic unit of religious and community life in medieval England

examples.en-GB: Most medieval people encountered the Church through their parish priest rather than bishops or the Pope.

data.targetWord: a legal court run by the Church that dealt with matters such as marriage, wills, moral behaviour and cases involving clergy

examples.en-GB: Henry II wanted criminal clergy tried in royal courts rather than church courts, which led to his conflict with Becket.

data.targetWord: King of England from 1189 to 1199, known as Richard the Lionheart, who led the Third Crusade against Saladin and became famous for his military leadership

examples.en-GB: Richard I fought Saladin during the Third Crusade but failed to recapture Jerusalem.

data.targetWord: the Pope who called the First Crusade in 1095 at the Council of Clermont, promising spiritual rewards to those who fought in the Holy Land

examples.en-GB: Pope Urban II's speech in 1095 inspired thousands of western Christians to take up the cross.

data.targetWord: Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 who defended the independence of the Church from royal interference and was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170

examples.en-GB: Thomas Becket's murder shocked Christian Europe and he was made a saint just three years later.

data.targetWord: the transfer of learning, ideas and goods between cultures that occurred during the Crusades, bringing Arab scholarship in medicine, mathematics and science to western Europe

examples.en-GB: The Crusades increased knowledge exchange between Europe and the Islamic world in medicine and astronomy.

data.title: Events in the Becket conflict in order
items: Henry II becomes king and seeks to strengthen royal justice
Becket becomes Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162
Becket defends Church courts and goes into exile
Becket returns to England; tensions continue
Four knights murder Becket in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170
Becket is made a saint in 1173
Henry II performs public penance at Canterbury in 1174

data.title: Key events of the First Crusade in order
items: Byzantine emperor asks the Pope for help against Turkish forces
Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095
Crusader States are established in the eastern Mediterranean

data.title: Events from First Crusade to end of Crusader rule — in order
items: Third Crusade led by Richard I fails to recapture Jerusalem
Acre falls in 1291, ending major Crusader rule

data.title: Sort Crusader motives into the correct category

pairs.text: Forgiveness of sins promised by the Pope
Protecting holy places such as Jerusalem
Obeying the call of the Pope as God's representative
Hope of gaining land or territory in the east
Search for honour and military reputation
Opportunity for younger sons with no inheritance

data.title: Types of Church power — sort each example into the correct category

pairs.text: Control over sacraments and people's hope of salvation
Belief in heaven, hell and purgatory shaped behaviour
Saints and miracles gave the Church spiritual authority
Collecting tithes gave the Church a large income
Church courts dealt with marriage and moral disputes
Bishops advised kings and held government offices
Popes could excommunicate or interdict kings
